title: Tries
tagline: Prefix trees that power autocomplete and spell-check — turning common-prefix queries into O(key length) lookups.

sections.content:
A **trie** (pronounced "try", from re**trie**val) is a tree-shaped data structure built specifically for strings. Unlike hash maps or BSTs that treat each key as an opaque unit, a trie decomposes every key into its individual characters and stores those characters along tree edges. Each path from the root to a marked node spells out a complete key.

The killer insight is **shared prefixes cost nothing extra**. Insert "cat", "car", and "card" and the first three characters `c → a → r` are stored once. That shared structure makes tries the natural choice for any prefix-based problem: autocomplete, spell-checking, IP routing tables, and phone-book lookup. Where a hash map gives O(k) insert/search (k = key length) but offers nothing about prefixes, a trie gives O(k) insert/search **and** O(p + n) prefix enumeration (p = prefix length, n = number of matches) — a capability no general-purpose hash map can match.

sections.title: A Physical Filing Cabinet
sections.content:
Imagine a library filing cabinet with 26 drawers, one per letter. Inside the `C` drawer is another 26-drawer cabinet; inside its `A` drawer is yet another — and so on, as deep as your longest word. To file the word "cat" you open drawer `C`, then `A`, then `T` and place a flag saying "word ends here".

To **search** for "car" you open `C → A → R` and check for the end-of-word flag — found in O(3) steps regardless of how many words are stored. To **autocomplete** the prefix "ca" you open `C → A` and then enumerate every path downward — that subtree contains every word starting with "ca". No scanning of unrelated words is necessary. This is the power that makes tries indispensable in search engines and mobile keyboard predictors.

Each trie node stores an array (or hash map) of **children** — one slot per possible next character — plus a boolean `isEnd` flag marking whether the path from root to this node spells a complete word.

**Insert** walks the string character by character, creating child nodes on demand, then sets `isEnd = true` at the final character. **Search** walks the same path; it returns `true` only if all characters are found **and** `isEnd` is set. **StartsWith** (prefix query) is identical but drops the `isEnd` requirement — any reachable endpoint suffices.

All three operations run in **O(k)** time where k is the key length, completely independent of the number of stored words. A hash map also achieves O(k) average search but cannot enumerate words by prefix without scanning all keys.

The main **cost** is space. A naive trie node with a 26-slot array wastes memory when most children are null. Two optimisations address this. A **compressed trie** (Patricia trie, radix tree) collapses chains of single-child nodes into single edges labelled with substrings — reducing node count at the cost of more complex code. A **ternary search trie (TST)** uses a BST-like structure per node — three children (less, equal, greater) instead of 26 — keeping the prefix-search advantage with far lower memory overhead. In production, hash-map children (`Map<char, TrieNode>`) strike a good balance: O(1) amortised child lookup, no wasted slots.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Using `Map` for children avoids wasting 26 slots per node. `#walk` shares path traversal across `search`, `startsWith`, and `autocomplete`. The `#dfs` helper enumerates all words in a subtree in O(output size) time after the O(prefix length) walk.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The delete routine uses post-order recursion to clean up leaf nodes that are no longer part of any word, preventing memory leaks. The longest-common-prefix algorithm walks the single-child chain — a classic trie interview problem solvable in O(total chars) time.

sections.content: **When an interview problem mentions prefixes, autocomplete, or word-by-word matching — think trie immediately.** A hash map cannot enumerate all words with a given prefix without scanning all keys. A trie does it in O(prefix length + number of results). Also remember: if the character set is small and fixed (lowercase a–z), an array of 26 children is slightly faster than a Map; if the character set is large or variable (Unicode, full ASCII), use a Map to avoid wasting memory.

items: A trie stores strings character by character along tree edges; each root-to-marked-node path spells a complete key.
Insert, search, and startsWith all run in O(k) where k is the key length — independent of the total number of stored words.
Autocomplete (prefix enumeration) runs in O(p + n): O(p) to reach the prefix node, O(n) to DFS the subtree.
The main trade-off is space: a naive 26-slot array per node wastes memory on sparse alphabets; Map-based children or compressed tries (radix trees) reduce overhead.
Tries are used in autocomplete engines, spell-checkers, IP routing (longest-prefix match), and DNA sequence search.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a word of length k into a trie?
options: O(log k)
O(k)
O(n) where n is number of stored words
O(k log n)
quiz.explanation: Insertion walks the word character by character, creating child nodes as needed. Each character step is O(1) with a Map or array of children, so the total cost is O(k) — the length of the word being inserted.

quiz.question: How does a trie's `search` differ from `startsWith`?
options: search is faster because it stops earlier
search checks the isEnd flag at the final node; startsWith does not
startsWith checks isEnd; search does not
There is no difference — both return the same result
quiz.explanation: Both traverse the same path character by character. `search` additionally requires that the final node has `isEnd = true`, meaning the path spells a complete stored word. `startsWith` returns true for any reachable endpoint — even if it's in the middle of a longer word.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of autocomplete — finding all words with a given prefix of length p when there are n matching words?
options: O(p)
O(n)
O(p + n)
O(p × n)
quiz.explanation: Autocomplete first walks the prefix in O(p) steps to reach the prefix node, then DFS-traverses the subtree visiting each character of each result exactly once — O(n) where n counts total characters in all matching words (often approximated as number of matches).

quiz.question: Why do tries use less memory than storing each word independently when many words share prefixes?
options: Tries compress each word with Huffman encoding
Tries store shared prefix characters in a single path rather than repeating them per word
Tries store only the suffix of each word after the longest common prefix
Tries use bitwise storage for each character
quiz.explanation: In a trie, the path `c → a → r` is stored once and shared by 'car', 'card', and 'care'. Each shared prefix character is a single node rather than a repeated character in separate string allocations.

quiz.question: Which data structure would you choose to find the longest word in a dictionary that is a prefix of a given query string?
options: Binary search tree sorted by word length
Hash map of all words
Trie — walk the query and track the last isEnd node
Sorted array with binary search
quiz.explanation: Walk the trie along the query string character by character, recording the depth of each node where `isEnd` is true. The deepest such node corresponds to the longest stored word that is a prefix of the query — solved in O(query length).

quiz.question: A trie node using an array of 26 children vs a Map — when is the array version preferred?
options: When the character set is large (e.g. full Unicode)
When memory is unlimited and the character set is small and fixed (e.g. lowercase a–z only)
When the trie stores numbers instead of strings
When the trie needs to support deletion
quiz.explanation: A 26-element array gives O(1) child access via `children[char - 'a']` with no hash overhead. It wastes memory when most slots are null, but for lowercase-only tries with many words the constant-time access and cache locality make it faster than a Map.

quiz.question: What real-world system uses a trie for longest-prefix matching in routing?
options: Database B-tree indexes
Internet routers matching IP addresses to destination networks
DNS round-robin load balancers
TLS certificate authorities
quiz.explanation: Internet routers store network prefixes (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) in a trie keyed on binary IP address bits. For each incoming packet the router walks the trie and takes the longest matching prefix — the most specific route. This is the classic trie application in networking.

quiz.question: What is a compressed trie (radix tree) and why is it used?
options: A trie stored in a compressed binary format on disk
A trie where chains of single-child nodes are merged into single edges with substring labels, reducing node count
A trie that only stores the first and last character of each word
A trie that uses binary rather than character-based branching
quiz.explanation: A radix tree collapses every chain of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with the shared substring. This reduces the number of nodes — and thus memory — significantly for sparse tries where many paths have no branching.

quiz.question: After deleting a word from a trie, when should a node actually be removed from memory?
options: Always immediately after clearing its isEnd flag
Only if it has no children and is not an end-of-word node for another word
After a full trie rebalance
Nodes are never removed — only isEnd flags are cleared
quiz.explanation: A node can be safely removed only when it is a leaf (no remaining children) and its isEnd flag is false. Removing it prematurely would break paths to other words that share the same prefix.

quiz.question: A trie stores 10 000 English words. What is the time complexity to find whether any stored word starts with the prefix 'inter'?
options: O(10 000) — must check all words
O(log 10 000) — binary search on sorted words
O(5) — length of 'inter'
O(5 × 10 000) — prefix check per word
quiz.explanation: Trie lookup is O(prefix length), completely independent of how many words are stored. Walking `i → n → t → e → r` is 5 steps regardless of whether the trie holds 100 or 10 million words.
